           RESPONSE BRIEF OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC

           Constellation1 submits this response brief to discuss three points with broad support in the

reply briefs regarding how PJM and the Transmission Owners2 must modify their proposals to

ensure compliance with the Commission’s December 18th Order.

           First, a proposed effective date of June 2029 runs counter to the spirit of the Commission’s

December 18th Order.3 PJM and Transmission Owners must act expeditiously. Winning the AI

race requires a sprint, not a stroll. The Commission could help accelerate the interconnection of

large loads by setting the new transmission services on separate tracks. Interim Network




1
    Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) submits this response in accordance with the hearing
    procedures established by the Commission in its December 18, 2025 Order. See PJM Interconnection, LLC, 193
    FERC ¶ 61,217, at P 220 (2025) (“December 18th Order”).
2

    Transmission Owners – avoiding a potentially protracted litigation over the precise rates avoids delay in

 Integration Transmission Service (“Interim NITS”)4 should go first and should be implemented by

October 1, 2026.

           Second, Interim NITS and Contract Demand Services should be fully supported, not made

“meaningless.”5 The Commission’s December 18th Order was a “landmark” order intended to

address the “urgent need ... that large loads are ‘able to connect to the transmission system in a

timely, orderly, and non-discriminatory manner.’”6 PJM and the Transmission Owners cannot

impose rates, terms and conditions that risk discrimination and render the new services so

unattractive that Network Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”) remains the only viable

option. New service terms and conditions must be just and reasonable.

           Without delay, the Commission should reject and direct further compliance on PJM’s and

the Transmission Owners’ proposals that restrict, discriminate, eliminate, or otherwise discourage

the new transmission services. PJM and the Transmission Owners’ initial briefs included several

provisions that would enable undue discrimination by Transmission Owners and continue to delay

large load interconnections. On reply, the Transmission Owners introduce several more. Two

simple solutions can prevent discrimination and delay: first, deadlines for deliverables from the

Transmission Owners, such as studies, and second, requiring standards, practices, and technical

requirements to be clear and on file at the Commission.

           Third, several critical terms of service need to be refined to make Interim NITS and

Contract Demand Services commercially workable. Before investing hundreds of millions of

whether the transmission services can be reliably provided and how loads will be curtailed. A lack

Consistent with the December 18th Order, the Commission should require these critical terms of

service to be stated clearly. We cannot afford continued setbacks from incremental or incomplete

proposals.

                                                          REPLY

     I.     Winning the AI Race Requires a Sprint, Not a Stroll

            A June 2029 effective date imposes a “three- to five- year moratorium” on the co-location

of large loads.8 This goes against the speedy interconnection that the Commission envisioned and

that is needed to win the AI race.9 Moreover, it allows rates found to be unjust and unreasonable—

that is, unlawful—to remain in place for three and a half more years, fundamentally undermining

the December 18th Order, not to mention the purpose of the Federal Power Act.10

    behalf of Co-Located Load.”).

Commission’s directives. Complete and clear proposals are needed for parties to provide comment

to ensure the new transmission services can work commercially as the Commission intended; that

is particularly necessary in this proceeding given the demonstrated history of discriminatory

            The Commission can accelerate interconnection of large loads by establishing separate

tracks for transmission services that can proceed on faster timelines.15 The Commission should

establish a separate track to promptly approve the rates and terms for Interim NITS, including the

study process, consistent with Constellation’s recommended modifications discussed below and

in prior pleadings. The effective date should be no later than October 1, 2026, as our

recommendations are targeted only at critical issues that would delay or otherwise render

meaningless the new transmission services. We have intentionally decided not to contest other

elements of PJM’s and the Transmission Owners’ proposals that potentially concern us, so as to

expeditiously complete these proceedings, timely implement new transmission services, and avoid

protracted litigation.16

  II.        New Transmission Services Should Be Supported, Not Discouraged or Made
            “Meaningless”

            The landmark December 18th Order directed PJM “to ensure that large loads are ‘able to

connect to the transmission system in a timely, orderly, and non-discriminatory manner.’”17 The

majority of commenters agree that PJM’s and the Transmission Owners’ proposals are

fundamentally at odds with the Commission’s directive.18 The proposals restrict, delay,

discriminate, or otherwise discourage the use of Interim NITS and Contract Demand Services. The

proposals produce the opposite effect of “releas[ing] the bottleneck of large load investments

across the PJM footprint”19 and are contrary to the core requirement in the Federal Power Act that

rates and terms be “just and reasonable.”20 Given the depth of PJM’s and the Transmission

Owners’ resistance,21 immediate Commission intervention is warranted. Without delay, the

                     A. The Commission Should Be on Guard for Opportunities that Allow for Undue
                        Discrimination and Continued Delay of Large Load-Interconnection.

            Numerous service terms proposed by PJM and the Transmission Owners introduce

opportunities for undue discrimination that have stifled competition and barred the timely

interconnection of loads to date.32 On reply, the Transmission Owners introduce several more,

including proposing to replace “Delivery Point” in the Illustrative Tariff with “Point of Change in

Ownership” to be “consistent” with PJM’s now-rejected definition of Co-Located Load and a host

of other proposals that could also give Transmission Owners unfettered discretion.33 The proposal

to replace “Delivery Point” with “Point of Change in Ownership” should be denied. Similar to

PJM’s rejected definition of Co-Located Load, using Point of Change in Ownership in the

Illustrative Tariff would risk “uncertainty or delays for parties in Co-Located Load

configurations.”34 To make the Illustrative Tariff consistent with the definition of Co-Located

Load, “Delivery Point” should be replaced with “Point of Interconnection.”

            The Commission should also act to mitigate the Transmission Owners’ new proposals that

could give them unfettered discretion over the timelines and technical requirements, including the

following Transmission Owner requests:

                •   “Tariff should specify that Transmission Owners’ load integration studies will be
                    completed first;”35

                •   “[T]he relevant Transmission Owner’s approval must be included in the process of
                    allowing service to be reinstated” after service was suspended;36

                •   “[T]echnical requirements should also require an Eligible Customer to satisfy any
                    applicable Transmission Owner-imposed technical requirements;”37

                •   “PJM Transmission Owners request that PJM add, as a condition precedent for
                    receiving service, that the Eligible Customer satisfy any load-connection related
                    requirements imposed by the applicable PJM Transmission Owner(s);”38 and

                •   “[T]he PJM Transmission Owners request that PJM add language to the list of
                    information to be provided in an application for Firm Contract Demand
                    Transmission Service and/or Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service to
                    the effect that the customer has met applicable load interconnection study
                    obligations.”39

           It is possible that some of these proposed requirements, with sufficient transparency,

standards and timelines, could be reasonable. However, without clarity with respect to the

obligations on Eligible Customers, Co-Located Generators, and the Transmission Owners that

currently function as gatekeepers for the implementation of these configurations, it is almost

certain that the expedition desired by the Commission in issuing this landmark order will not be

First, the Commission can direct PJM to establish deadlines for studies and other Transmission

procedures.41 PJM should be able to adopt them here.

             Second, the Commission should require PJM’s and Transmission Owners’ standards,

requirements, guidance, and practices on Co-Location Arrangements to be on file with the

Commission on a standalone basis or reflected in PJM’s Tariff.42 Rules for Co-Location

Arrangements must be clearly stated and available as they “significantly affect rates, terms and

conditions” of service and can be “readily susceptible to specification.”43 They cannot be hidden

and subject to unilateral change without any notice or without any Commission oversight.44

            In particular, the study process and standards applicable to Interim NITS requests should

be the first priority. Interim NITS should be the easiest of the various new transmission services

to implement for the reasons Constellation has discussed previously.45 Furthermore, many co-

location requests are for front of the meter NITS, for which an Interim NITS option would provide

immediate relief. PJM’s omission of any detail with respect to this study process does not comply

with the Commission’s directive to provide additional record evidence to set the appropriate

replacement rates, terms and conditions for Interim NITS.46 The Commission should direct PJM

to file its study process for Interim NITS within 30 days.

          II.      PURPOSE OF SPECIAL PROTECTION SCHEMES AND PROCESS FOR SELECTING
                   APPROPRIATE REMEDIATION

4.              The reply comments by Indicated Transmission Owners imply three incorrect

assumptions about special protection schemes: (1) the purpose of special protection schemes is to

“ensure that a Co-Located Load does not exceed its specified level of transmission service,”3 that

is, to deter unreserved use; (2) special protection schemes “must be implemented”4 for all Co-

Location Arrangements to maintain reliability; and (3) special protection schemes should be

required on “both the customer’s side and the Transmission Owner’s side of the point of

interconnection.”5 Below, I rebut each assumption in turn while explaining the purpose of special

protection schemes and how PJM currently determines their necessity.

5.              First, the purpose of special protection schemes is not to deter unreserved use of the

transmission system. That is the purpose of penalties. Special protection schemes are intended to

maintain reliability by protecting the system from actual overloads and conditions that could

cause cascading failures that PJM cannot mitigate through normal operations. They are not

intended to manage contractual requirements or mitigate conditions that PJM can manage

through normal operations, such as contingency overloads that can be tolerated based on a four-

6.         Second, requiring special protection schemes by default for every Co-Location

Arrangement is not good utility practice. While special protection schemes are commonly used,7

special protection schemes (above and beyond normal equipment protection) are not appropriate

for every situation. This is because the technical studies that PJM conducts, which form the basis

for remediation, do not always show that an interconnection request could result in a criteria

violation that could lead to severe actual overloads and the need for immediate or instantaneous

response to maintain reliability. Requirements for special protections schemes should reflect the

basic principle that we should not require interventions that add technical complexity to the

system when such interventions are not necessary, e.g., when the reliability risks do not merit

such interventions. In short, special protection schemes should only be implemented when

necessary.

special protection schemes on “both the customer’s side and the Transmission Owner’s side of

interconnection of load could lead to an actual overload and in such cases a special protection

scheme would be inadvisable. Double special protection schemes may be appropriate in some

circumstances where the risks are so severe that redundancy is critical, but as I discuss below,

      III.      A FAIR AND TRANSPARENT PROCESS FOR DETERMINING REMEDIATION MEASURES

12.          I understand that PJM has not articulated the studies it will perform on Co-Located Load

arrangements that would be the basis for determining the appropriate remediation necessary to

maintain system reliability. Without additional clarification, PJM risks further delaying the

interconnection of large loads and the potential of parties studying “extreme cases” to simply show

                                                    6
 violations, not actual reliability and stability risks. To ensure a fair and transparent process, PJM

should develop a Co-Located Load request study process leveraging its existing generator

interconnection study process and RTEP process as models.

13.         Three principles should guide PJM in adapting its existing processes. First, system studies

of unauthorized use should be standardized, transparent, and based on reasonable assumptions set

ahead of time (and not guided by an opaque process and rules that differ from Transmission Owner

to Transmission Owner). Like the generator interconnection study process, the study process for

Co-Located Loads should be PJM-driven where most of the studies are all done based on RTO-

wide processes and Transmission Owners have to justify any exception they require.

14.         Second, PJM should develop criteria for PJM to assess system performance to establish

acceptable/unacceptable levels of risk. These criteria should be based on the existing NERC and

Regional standards used today to assess reliability risk.

15.         Third, remediation should be commensurate with the level of risk identified in the studies.

If the studies show no reliability issues, then no additional remediation should be required. This is

not to say there is no protection. Interconnection facilities typically always include general

protection schemes, such as equipment protection relaying and control devices.

      IV.      ADDITIONAL MEASURES TO ENSURE RELIABILITY

16.         Some may argue that because planning models may not capture all possible situations that

could present a reliability risk (which is true for all planning analysis), PJM should require special

protection scheme for all Co-Location Arrangements. While some scenarios may go unstudied,

the solution to ensuring adequate reliability and stability is not to over-mitigate. Rather, PJM

should monitor in real-time and adjust remediation as necessary. Real-time monitoring is standard

for a system operator. In fact, PJM proposes to monitor the Co-Located Load demand on the



                                                     7
 Transmission System.9 Real-time monitoring of Co-Located Load should also be simple for PJM

to implement. Most standard metering equipment can provide real time telemetry. PJM needs to

add the individual load and generation to the model and set-up the standard communications to

receive the data. PJM already has standard process to do both on a routine basis. Including these

resources should be no different than adding any other facility to the models.
